description:
## Motivation

The web sockets example was not looking nice, it was not user-friendly at all (took a while to figure out what it was even supposed to be able to do). Furthermore, it was not actually showcasing anything about web sockets that the chat example did not already demonstrate better.  Either it had to go, or it had to be made more distinct, so I took the time to make it more "involved". 

## Solution

-  all parts of the example have received additional comments
- the sample webpage has received hints that the user should open browser's console to see messages (it was just blank)
- added a Python script that demonstrates some more tricky features such as ping/pong handling, and allows to quickly connect with multiple "users" to the test server
- added the logic to push unsolicited messages to the client form the server (which is not obvious at all though easy to actually do)
- added comments explaining that one should not try to implement pong responder (as axum already has one builtin, and thus even though you can see the ping messages, you should not actually respond to them)

> examples must be about axum only

I didn't say that. I said they should be related to axum. For example a while ago someone submitted a PR with an sqlx example that included a whole setup for migrations. But migrations aren't related to axum so they don't need to be in the example.

I think there is value in being able to open the browser and see data coming in from the websocket. Having a 9 line JS file for that is totally fine.

TL;DR version:
- tungstenite example is very "shallow" and only shows how *one* client would interact with the server, which is already demonstrated well enough by the browser example.
- I wanted specifically do demonstrate how one could lay groundwork for more complex/non-standard state machines with multiple concurrent flows, rather than the beaten to death chat example. It would be tough to demonstrate with a silly client.

The entire idea I had with conceptual improvements to the example  was to really show good reasons one would want to use Axum implementation in particular if compared to, for example, actix. For me personally the key reason is specifically how one can have independent send and receive logic for the websockets, and how all of that can be 100% async-aware, and with minimal boilerplate. For contrast, in Actix the expectation is that one either

-  handles messages as "copy types", which means they are fully buffered before feeding them into a handler using their Actor model, or, alternatively, 
- or uses their low-level API, which is "fun", and you'd have to handle things like ping/pong yourself which is ugly. [https://github.com/actix/examples/blob/master/websockets/chat-actorless/src/handler.rs#L54](as they show in their own examples)

Well every websocket open is an HTTP request, so before we can get to websocket stuff proper we need to have a handler for the original HTTP request, which that function is. Which is why it is the last place where HTTP headers can be seen, and after that we are essentially talking in another protocol. In this sense it is a "formality" if all you wanted was websockets.
